title: The Thunder of His Voice
summary: Elihu's final words describe a storm as it breaks. God's voice thunders, his lightning flashes to the ends of the earth, snow and rain fall at his command, animals take shelter, and ice forms by his breath. Elihu then turns to Job with a string of questions about the clouds and the skies that no human can answer, and he ends by describing God coming out of the north in golden splendor, beyond reach, great in power and justice.
story: This chapter completes Elihu's fourth speech, begun in chapter 36, and closes his long contribution to the book. It also closes the whole human side of the debate. Job, the three friends, and Elihu have all spoken, and each has tried in his own way to account for God. Elihu's last words point beyond himself: a storm is gathering, and he is overwhelmed by it. The very next verse of the book, at the start of chapter 38, says that the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind. Elihu's questions to Job in verses 14 to 20 also anticipate the form of God's speech, which will consist almost entirely of questions about creation that Job cannot answer.
historical:
The chapter's background is the climate and religion of the ancient Near East. In the lands around Israel, the storm was the clearest display of divine power, and storm gods held a leading place among the gods. In the Canaanite texts discovered at Ugarit on the Syrian coast, written before 1200 BC, Baal is the storm god who thunders with his voice, rides the clouds, and gives the rain on which life depends. His home is Mount Zaphon, a mountain in the north. Mesopotamia had its own storm god, Adad.

Elihu's description takes up this familiar imagery and gives all of it to the one God. It is God, not Baal, whose voice thunders and who commands the rain, and verse 22 says that out of the north (the Hebrew word is tsaphon) he comes in golden splendor. Israel's poets did this more than once; Psalm 29, with its repeated voice of the LORD over the waters, is the closest parallel. The effect for an ancient reader was to strip the storm of any rival divinity. The thunder is simply the voice of the Creator.
cultural:
For people who worked the land, the weather was not background but life and death. Snow and heavy rain stopped work in the fields (verse 7 says God seals up the hand of every man), drove animals into their dens, and forced households to wait. The south wind that makes clothes hot (verse 17) is the hot, dry wind from the desert known across the region, which brings stifling heat. The sky spread out like a mirror of bronze (verse 18) reflects the ancient practice of making mirrors from polished metal rather than glass, and pictures the hard, shining dome of a cloudless summer sky.

Verse 13 introduces a word the Old Testament uses for God's covenant loyalty, chesed. In a world that often read storms and floods as signs of divine anger, Elihu insists that the same weather can serve three purposes: discipline, the good of the land, and God's steadfast love. The storm isn't random; it is sent.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 13 are a vivid, present-tense description of a storm, with Elihu reporting his own trembling heart as though the thunder were sounding while he speaks. The repeated word voice (verses 2, 4, and 5) ties the storm to speech: God's thunder is God talking. Verses 14 to 24 turn to direct address. Elihu calls Job to stand still and consider, then asks a series of questions (Do you know? Do you understand? Can you?) that no human can answer. The chapter ends not with Elihu's argument but with a vision of God coming in majesty. Many readers see this structure as a hinge: Elihu starts to ask the kind of questions that God will now ask far more fully.

outline.t: Snow, rain, ice, and cloud obey his command
God comes in golden splendor, beyond reach

doctrines.note: God directs the weather: snow, rain, whirlwind, and cloud accomplish all that he commands over the face of the earth. Elihu names three purposes for which he sends them, punishment, the good of his land, and his loving devotion, so that nature itself serves God's moral purposes.

God is beyond our reach, exalted in power, and in his justice and great righteousness he does not oppress. Elihu holds together transcendence and goodness: God's greatness is not the greatness of a tyrant.
The storm is described as God's voice. Creation speaks of its maker, and the thunder prepares Job, and the reader, for the moment when God will speak in words.

words.note: Qol, voice or sound, also the ordinary Hebrew word for thunder. In verses 2 to 5 it means both at once: the rumbling of the storm is the voice of God. The same double sense runs through Psalm 29, and it sets up the next chapter, where God's voice will speak from the storm.

Chesed, steadfast love, loyal kindness, or loving devotion, one of the richest words in the Old Testament and usually tied to God's covenant faithfulness. Its appearance in verse 13, in the middle of a storm, is striking: God sends the rain not only in judgment or for the land but out of his loyal love.

Tsaphon, north. The word is also the name of Mount Zaphon, the mountain in the north where Canaanite poetry placed the home of the storm god Baal. When verse 22 says God comes out of the north in golden splendor, a first reader might have heard a claim that the true God, not Baal, is lord of the storm mountain.

Suphah, whirlwind or storm wind. In verse 9 the tempest comes from its chamber. The imagery of the storm wind here prepares directly for the whirlwind (a different Hebrew word with a similar sense) out of which the LORD speaks in 38:1.

christ: Elihu ends with a God beyond reach, coming in unapproachable majesty. The Gospels show that same authority over the storm in a man in a boat. When Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea on the lake of Galilee, his disciples asked, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41). Their question makes sense only against chapters like this one, in which the thunder, the wind, and the waters obey God alone. The link is not a prediction in Elihu's words; it is the New Testament recognizing in Jesus the one whose voice commands creation. The God who seemed beyond reach has come near.

hard.q: Does God cause every storm and natural disaster?
hard.a:
Elihu speaks as though God directly commands every snowfall and lightning strike, and much of the Old Testament speaks the same way. Readers have understood this in different ways. Many Christians, in the Reformed tradition especially, hold that God's providence governs all events, including natural ones, though through ordinary causes and for purposes we often can't see. Others emphasize that creation has a genuine freedom and regularity of its own, and that the Bible's language of God sending rain and snow affirms his ultimate rule without making him the immediate cause of each event in a mechanical sense.

What Elihu adds is purpose: storms may come for discipline, for the good of the land, or from God's steadfast love. He does not claim anyone can tell which is which in a given case. The book of Job as a whole warns against reading any particular disaster as a verdict on the people it strikes; Job's own children died in a storm (1:19), and the reader knows it was not their punishment.

questions: Elihu hears the thunder as the voice of God. What in the natural world most makes you aware of God's greatness?
Verse 13 says God can send the storm for punishment, for his land, or in his loving devotion. How does it change your view of hardship to think that God's purposes might be more than one?
Elihu asks Job questions he cannot answer. Why might being confronted with the limits of our knowledge be a gift rather than a humiliation?
